questions.subject: History
questions.prompt: A student says the fall of Rome in 476 CE happened suddenly and out of nowhere, with no warning signs beforehand. What's wrong with this view?
options: It ignores centuries of gradual decline from economic trouble, invasions, and political instability before 476 CE
Rome actually fell in 1096 CE, not 476 CE
Rome never fell, it just changed its name to the Byzantine Empire
The fall was caused entirely by a single volcanic eruption
questions.answer: It ignores centuries of gradual decline from economic trouble, invasions, and political instability before 476 CE
questions.why: 476 CE marks a symbolic endpoint, but the Western Roman Empire had been weakening for a long time due to economic strain, repeated invasions, and internal political chaos. The 'sudden collapse' idea is a common oversimplification.

questions.subject: History
questions.prompt: A student thinks lords could do whatever they wanted with no obligations to anyone. What did a lord actually owe to the king or a higher lord in the feudal system?
options: Military service and loyalty in exchange for holding their land
Nothing — lords had no obligations to anyone above them
Only money, never military support
A yearly religious pilgrimage to Rome
questions.answer: Military service and loyalty in exchange for holding their land
questions.why: Feudalism was a two-way chain of obligation — even powerful lords held their land from someone above them (usually the king) and owed loyalty and military service in return. No one was truly obligation-free.

questions.subject: English
questions.prompt: A student claims Romeo and Juliet was written for a modern theatre audience with electric lighting and microphones. What does this overlook about how the play was originally performed?
options: It was performed in open-air Elizabethan theatres relying on daylight and the actors' own voices
It was originally performed as a silent film
It was first performed on television
It was written to be read privately and never performed on stage
questions.answer: It was performed in open-air Elizabethan theatres relying on daylight and the actors' own voices
questions.why: Elizabethan theatres like the Globe had no electric lighting or amplification — plays were performed in daylight, outdoors, with actors projecting their voices to reach the crowd.

questions.subject: English
questions.prompt: A student says Shakespeare's use of the balcony scene is only about romance and has no deeper technique behind it. What technique-based feature makes this scene more than 'just romance'?
options: Shakespeare uses light/dark imagery and dramatic irony to build tension about the lovers' secrecy and danger
The scene is written entirely in prose to show it's unimportant
The scene has no dialogue, only stage directions
It was added by a later editor and isn't Shakespeare's original work
questions.answer: Shakespeare uses light/dark imagery and dramatic irony to build tension about the lovers' secrecy and danger
questions.why: The balcony scene layers in imagery (light vs dark) and dramatic irony (the audience knows the danger the lovers don't fully grasp) — techniques that deepen the romance into something tense and foreboding.

questions.subject: English
questions.prompt: A student thinks the 'love vs hate' theme only shows up when characters are being affectionate. Which of these best shows the theme working through conflict, not affection?
options: The feud between the Capulets and Montagues fuels violence that ultimately destroys the young lovers
Romeo and Juliet's wedding, which shows only their love
The Nurse's jokes with Juliet, which show only comic relief
The Prince's opening speech, which is purely about law and order
questions.answer: The feud between the Capulets and Montagues fuels violence that ultimately destroys the young lovers
questions.why: Love vs hate isn't just about romantic scenes — the ongoing family hatred directly drives the tragedy, showing how love and hate are intertwined throughout the whole plot, not just in loving moments.

questions.subject: Science
questions.prompt: In an experiment testing how the amount of water given to plants affects their growth height, a student mixes up which variable is dependent. What is the dependent variable here?
options: The height of the plants, since it's the outcome being measured
The amount of water given, since it's what's measured
The type of soil used, since it changes the results
The number of plants tested, since it varies
questions.answer: The height of the plants, since it's the outcome being measured
questions.why: The dependent variable is what you measure as the outcome — here, plant height. The amount of water is the independent variable, the thing being deliberately changed.

questions.subject: Science
questions.prompt: A student claims that only plants can reproduce asexually, and all animals must reproduce sexually. Which organism proves this wrong?
options: Starfish, which can regenerate and reproduce asexually from a fragment
Humans, who always reproduce sexually
Dogs, who always reproduce sexually
Elephants, who always reproduce sexually
questions.answer: Starfish, which can regenerate and reproduce asexually from a fragment
questions.why: Many animals, not just plants, can reproduce asexually — starfish are a classic example, capable of regenerating a whole new individual from just a fragment of their body.

questions.subject: History
questions.prompt: A student says the Crusades were fought only between Christians and Muslims, with no other groups involved. What does this overlook about who was actually affected or involved?
options: Jewish communities and Eastern Christians (Byzantines) were also significantly affected and sometimes targeted
The Crusades only ever involved European kings fighting each other
The Crusades were entirely a naval conflict with no land battles
No civilians were ever affected by the Crusades
questions.answer: Jewish communities and Eastern Christians (Byzantines) were also significantly affected and sometimes targeted
questions.why: The Crusades' impact went beyond a simple Christian-vs-Muslim frame — Jewish communities faced violence during Crusader campaigns, and the Byzantine (Eastern Christian) Empire was also drawn into and damaged by Crusader actions, notably during the Fourth Crusade.

questions.subject: History
questions.prompt: A student says that once Rome fell, Europe had no functioning governments at all until the Renaissance. What actually filled the political gap in the early medieval period?
options: Local kingdoms and the feudal system, where lords and kings held regional power
The Roman Senate continued ruling from Rome unchanged
The United Nations stepped in to govern Europe
Europe had no political structure of any kind for a thousand years
questions.answer: Local kingdoms and the feudal system, where lords and kings held regional power
questions.why: Rome's fall didn't create a total political vacuum — smaller kingdoms and the feudal system emerged, giving regional lords and kings structured (if fragmented) control over territory and people.

questions.subject: English
questions.prompt: A student insists Shakespeare wrote Romeo and Juliet as an entirely original story with no earlier sources. What does this get wrong?
options: Shakespeare based it on earlier existing stories and poems about doomed lovers, adapting rather than inventing the plot from scratch
Shakespeare invented every plot element with no outside influence
The story was first written by Shakespeare's daughter
The play was based on a real event Shakespeare witnessed personally
questions.answer: Shakespeare based it on earlier existing stories and poems about doomed lovers, adapting rather than inventing the plot from scratch
questions.why: Shakespeare drew on earlier sources, including Arthur Brooke's narrative poem, reshaping existing material into his own dramatic version rather than creating the story entirely from nothing.

questions.subject: English
questions.prompt: A student thinks foreshadowing in Romeo and Juliet is only found in the prologue and nowhere else in the play. Which moment later in the play also clearly foreshadows the tragic ending?
options: Romeo's line before the Capulet party, sensing 'some consequence yet hanging in the stars'
The Nurse's comic story about Juliet as a baby
Mercutio's joke about Queen Mab's chariot being made of nutshells
The servants' brawl in the opening street scene
questions.answer: Romeo's line before the Capulet party, sensing 'some consequence yet hanging in the stars'
questions.why: Foreshadowing appears throughout the play, not just in the prologue — Romeo's own sense of dread before meeting Juliet hints at the tragic fate awaiting them, reinforcing the 'star-crossed' theme.

questions.subject: History
questions.prompt: A classmate says the Crusades were a total failure because Jerusalem was eventually lost again. Explain to them, in your own reasoning, why historians still see the Crusades as historically significant despite this military failure — think beyond who controlled the city.
